Taiwan holds local elections under Beijing's watchful gaze

Taiwan is electing local leaders across 22 cities and counties on Saturday amid accusations by Taiwanese authorities of attempts by China to interfere and sow distrust in the island-nation’s electoral system. Chinese authorities reject the allegations.

Taiwan is choosing mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties in an election Saturday that will test whether the ruling party can notch some wins at the local level.

Polls opened at 8am and are set to close at 4pm Results normally are tallied and announced the same day. Winners will serve four-year terms.

Unlike presidential elections, when relations with China and Beijing’s pressure on the island are major issues, Saturday’s vote is focused more on local concerns, including social welfare benefits and other issues affecting people’s daily lives.

But China has not been entirely absent from the debate. Taiwanese authorities have accused Beijing of attempting to sow distrust in the island’s electoral system, allegations that Chinese authorities have rejected.

Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense counted some 33 sorties from China's People’s Liberation Army warplanes between Friday and Saturday flying toward Taiwan, including bombers and fighter jets.

Read moreTaiwan launches annual war games as pressure from China grows

Saturday's elections feature candidates mostly from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party or the Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang or KMT. Traditionally, the KMT has performed well in local elections. In 2022, the DPP won in only five out of 22 localities.

Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te has campaigned for DPP candidates, appearing Thursday night to support his party’s mayoral candidate in Taoyuan City.

Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy, which Beijing claims. Ahead of its elections, its government warned the public to be vigilant of any fake claims on social media, citing continuous Chinese disinformation efforts.

The capital Taipei is traditionally a KMT stronghold, but the DPP’s mayoral candidate Puma Shen has been viewed as a strong challenger to incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an.

Other notable races are in New Taipei City and Kaohsiung. New Taipei City’s incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung’s mayoral office is held by the DPP.

A third party, the Taiwan People’s Party, is running in some smaller races and supports the KMT’s candidate in the Taipei mayoral race.

Across Taipei, colorful banners promoting each candidate blanket the otherwise dull brown and gray surfaces of buildings.

Voter Chang Li-fen went to her Taipei polling place early Saturday morning. Declining to name the candidate, she said she voted for the person she thinks will be the best for the economy.

“If the Taiwan economy is good, only then will people be able to live well,” she said. “In France and in Italy, people are protesting because of energy costs, which raised the cost of living, so I think the economy is most important.”

Candidates held rallies Friday in a last-minute bid for votes.

Puma Shen traveled in a motorcade across the city stopping for 15 minutes at a time to greet the crowds of supporters lining the street, many of whom came ahead of time to specific spots his campaign had outlined on a map.

Incumbent Chiang Wan-an held a rally with supporters at night with other KMT city council members, with his supporters waving balloons, flags and light-up sticks to cheer him on.

Elon Musk can afford a little MAGA amnesia

His failed bet on the Republicans has done nothing to diminish the bipartisan appeal of his fortune.

Following the dismal performance of the Republican Party in the United States midterm elections this month, the world’s richest person, Elon Musk, admitted that he felt “pretty foolish about having spent so much money” backing Republican candidates.

The CEO of Tesla and SpaceX dropped almost $500m on elections that saw Democrats sweep Congress. Granted, this isn’t exactly “so much money” for someone whose net worth hovers in the vicinity of $820bn.

Musk furthermore took the opportunity to announce that he is not, in fact, a disciple of US President Donald Trump’s signature Make America Great Again movement: “I’m not MAGA.”

This was a curious statement, no doubt, coming from a man who in very recent history has been known to sport MAGA hats and say things like: “I’m not just MAGA. I’m dark, gothic MAGA.”

Now, however, he has ditched the MAGA hat, explaining that he is not even “sure what MAGA means”. If it happens to mean a “sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party”, he remarked, “then I certainly don’t have that”.

Anyway, who needs “blind adherence” when you already have more money than anyone else on the planet?

To be sure, Musk has backed Democrats in the past, including former presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden. During his brief but dramatic breakup last year with Trump – for whose 2024 electoral victory Musk claims personal credit – various members of the Democratic camp jumped at the chance to woo Musk and his money back to their side.

And the bipartisan commitment to plutocracy is something that won’t be defeated in any US election any time soon.

After Trump reassumed power last January, Musk was granted a post at the head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), where he promptly went about dismantling government agencies and seeing to it that masses of federal workers lost their jobs – all the while personally benefiting from his own companies’ government contracts.

In his post-MAGA political reinvention, Musk has spontaneously cast himself as “ideologically quite moderate” – which might be news to anyone who associates ideological moderation with ideas such as workers having rights and that the world should not be governed by a handful of zillionaire sociopaths.

As Jim Naureckas, editor of the New York-based outlet Fairness & Accuracy In Reporting, said to me regarding the basis of Musk’s business model: “Elon Musk has amassed unfathomable wealth by convincing people that his not very profitable companies would some day make insane profits.”

As Naureckas put it, Musk in turn used that fortune “to ally himself with the ugliest elements of national and world politics, taking an active part in the looting and corrupting of the US government”. But now that the movement Musk enthusiastically hitched his wagon to is in disgrace, “he’s frantically trying to rebrand himself” despite having been “Sieg-Heiling the second Trump inauguration” a mere two years ago.

By coincidence, Musk has determined that the Democratic governor-elect of the state of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, is “quite moderate” – just like him! – so hopefully they’ll find some way to coexist in harmonious “moderation”. Texas, of course, is where Tesla and SpaceX have their headquarters, and where Musk had thus directed a significant portion of his “pretty foolish” campaign donations to ensure continued friendly Republican dominance.

Trump, for his part, had a rather less apoplectic reaction than one might have expected to Musk apparently jumping ship, telling NBC News: “He’s a friend of mine.”

This was far more cordial, at least, than the presidential tantrum that transpired after last year’s falling-out, when Trump declared Musk “so depressed and heartbroken” at having lost his post at DOGE that he was even suffering from “Trump derangement syndrome” – whatever that means.

As for what MAGA means, Musk may claim to no longer understand the significance of the movement he aided and abetted, but Trump has it quite clear: “I mean, you have to ask—there are lots of definitions out there. MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.”

Good to have that straightened out.

Musk is not the only grotesquely rich and influential person to distance himself from MAGA in the aftermath of the midterms. There’s also the likes of Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir – the tech firm that has been fundamental to Trump’s deportation binge and other mass abuses – who is now claiming to be a “progressive”.

But as the post-electoral rebrandings and semantic acrobatics carry on, it’s worth recalling that, MAGA or no MAGA, the US has never been a place where humane ideals have been permitted to thrive. Basic rights to healthcare, shelter, and education are converted into prohibitively expensive luxuries while the military goes about terrorising other countries willy-nilly and sending billions of dollars in charitable contributions to Israel’s genocide in the Gaza Strip.

Meanwhile, Elon Musk is able to throw away hundreds of millions of dollars and then shrug it off as “pretty foolish”.

According to Musk, Republican midterm losses are an indication that “American elections are not just about money”.

But the thing about plutocracy is, everything is always about money. And whatever hat Musk decides to don next is not going to change that.

item.title: Defense company Chemring protects NATO fleets. Here's why an activist investor wants it to break up
item.description:

U.K. defense group Chemring owns assets critical to NATO's weapons supply chain. But one activist hedge fund is pushing for the breakup of the group, which it says is failing to fully capitalize on soaring military spending. A strategic overhaul of the company, including the sale of Chemring's electronic warfare unit Roke, would generate up to 80% upside in the stock, according to Palliser Capital. London-listed Chemring has a £1.55 billion ($1.9 billion) market cap. Palliser — which manages about $1.6 billion in assets, focusing on opportunities mainly in Europe and Asia — is a top 10 shareholder, with a near-3% stake. Chemring's two core businesses — countermeasures and energetics — occupy strategically important positions in the global defense industry, with "indispensable assets at the heart of the munitions supply chain," James Smith, Palliser founder and chief investment officer, told the Sohn London investment conference on Nov. 18. CHG-GB 1M mountain Chemring. Its countermeasures divisions provide flares and decoys to protect military jets and naval vessels, while its energetics business produces high-end explosives and rocket motors. Together, they account for about 65% of group revenues. The company protected a huge proportion of NATO's air fleet, 85% according to Palliser's and Chemring's numbers, and 60% of the alliance's naval fleet. "They're Europe's largest player in HMX [high melting explosive] and the only major independent supplier of scale high-end explosives," Smith said. Chemring should be benefiting from a multiyear rearmament cycle, according to Smith, with depleted stockpiles and growing missile demand creating acute supply shortages. The group, whose full-year results are due Dec. 8, reported a record £1.4 billion ($1.8 billion) order book as of Oct. 31, up from £1.3 billion a year earlier. However, earnings growth has lagged defense peers, according to Smith. Its compound annual sales growth rate is a lofty 17%, but earnings before interest and taxes have fallen from 24% to 14%, which Smith said was actually closer to 7% when R & D tax credits are taken into account. Smith said the solution would be to sell off Roke, the group's specialist engineering, data and cyberwarfare consultancy business. Roke lacks synergies with the group's manufacturing operations and would be better suited to an owner with greater scale and reach, he added. Proceeds from the sale could be used to accelerate investment in energetics, expand manufacturing capacity and pursue growth opportunities in the U.S. and allied markets. Smith said such steps could put Chemring's valuation at between £8.34 and £9.16 per share, representing up to 80% upside over 12 months. And the timing could be particularly opportune amid an ongoing CEO transition. Chemring CEO Michael Ord will retire on Jan. 1, 2027, when CEO-designate Tom Newman, who joined in October, takes over after 17 years at defense rival Babcock . Smith said Palliser had identified other hedge funds, private equity sponsors and strategic investors interested in the opportunity. Together with Palliser, those investors account for more than 25% of Chemring's shareholder register, he added. A Chemring spokesperson told CNBC: "We welcome engagement with our shareholders but do not comment on media or market speculation."

Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks

The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.

Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.

The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.

Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.

"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.

He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.

Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.

Pressing need for workers, but hesitant to hire

Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.

A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.

Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly Germany's renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), are reluctant to recruit from places like India, say observers.

"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively new concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," said Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.

The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja said.

This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.

Language a key hurdle

Saikia, the butcher, had studied German to the B1 level, considered intermediate proficiency. He soon realized it was not enough for everyday communication at work.

"Initially, I found the theory classes of my Ausbildung quite difficult. But my co-workers helped me. After one year, my German improved, and I realized integration happened automatically as my language level improved," he said.

David Kipp, researcher in the Global Issues Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said he's "skeptical" about lowering language requirements.

"Language skills are an important selection criterion so people actually know where they are going. Sending people with very little language knowledge makes exploitation easier, because they have less direct contact with German institutions," he told DW.

Language, however, isn't the only hurdle.

Raja said workers' councils also often resist hiring from abroad.

"Company decisions in the Mittelstand involve the team and the shop floor," he pointed out. "In some cases, the workers' council resists hiring from India because they mistakenly believe 'cheap Indian labor' will take their jobs or undercut their wages."

Raja said he often uses unconventional outreach methods, including hosting TikTok Live sessions, to engage directly with industrial employers and workers and dispel concerns and misconceptions.

Exploiting the EU mobility loophole?

German companies have traditionally relied on workers from Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations such as Poland, Romania and Slovenia to fill labor market gaps.

But studies show CEE workers are increasingly reluctant to relocate to Germany, as faster economic growth and stronger career prospects improve opportunities in their home countries.

The situation has prompted recruitment agencies in these countries to look beyond the European Union for workers.

These third-country nationals (TCNs) obtain residence permits in CEE states and are then posted to German job sites under the Vander Elst visa. The mechanism allows non-EU citizens legally employed in one EU member state to be temporarily sent to work in another.

"European Labour Authority's (ELA) 2025 study on the posting of third-country nationals found that the number of posted TCNs is increasing. The main sectors concerned are construction and transport," said Pia Fallstrom, ELA spokesperson.

The exact number of TCNs posted across the EU is difficult to gauge, as data exchange between sending and receiving countries by nationality and sector is limited.

"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.

While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.

"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.

"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits."…

US military cloud platform reportedly hacked as Pentagon insists systems are secure

Hackers reportedly breached the US Air Force's Cloud One platform late Friday, potentially exposing sensitive military data. The Pentagon did not specifically deny that the system had been accessed, but insists its networks remain secure amid an ongoing spate of cyber-related data incidents.

The US military on Friday denied any issues with its computer security following media reports that the Air Force's cloud based system was hacked, in what would be the latest high profile breach of US digital infrastructure in recent weeks.

Asked whether the Air Force's Cloud One platform had been hacked, the Pentagon did not specifically deny that the system had been breached.

Instead, a Defense Department official told AFP late Friday that "The Department of War's systems are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world. We will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications."

"As a matter of policy and operations security, the Department of War does not comment on the status of our networks," a Defense Department official said earlier on Friday.

NBC News, a major US broadcaster, reported Friday citing an unnamed US official, that the cloud platform had been breached and that an attack "could have exposed sensitive military information."

The breach was first reported by Reuters earlier Friday.

Federal News Network, which specialises in covering US federal agencies, also confirmed the breach, citing a "person familiar with the incident."

The contractors discovered the hack earlier in the year while doing maintenance on the system, Federal News said.

The reported attack is the latest in a string of major outages in US government and private-sector digital infrastructure.

In recent weeks the CIA and FBI were also reportedly subject to hacks.

Suppliers for major American financial institutions including JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard were also hit.

In other instances, such as a major Microsoft Outlook outage, a separate US air traffic control issue and a reported issue with a top-secret National Security Agency (NSA) network earlier this month, officials were at pains to blame the outages on maintenance or defects – not intrusions.

item.title: Saudi Arabia shifts Vision 2030 spending amid economic and security pressure
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Saudi Arabia's economic diversification strategy has moved from "spending and delivery at any cost" to "spending and delivery at the right cost," Economy Minister Faisal Alibrahim told CNBC on Friday.

It comes after the Kingdom scaled back or cut several flagship projects as it endures a sharp economic contraction.

Alibrahim also said Saudi Arabia would "stop at nothing from realizing long-term sustainable stability in the region" amid ongoing Houthi strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure that have killed and injured dozens and repeatedly rocked oil markets.

"The phase we're in today is one where every riyal is deployed with greater precision... it was clear that while we want to diversify or restructure our economy to depend less on government spend, there was a lot of catch-up that needed to be done, and for that, you saw government spend leading the way," Alibrahim told CNBC's Dan Murphy.

"Right now, that is shifting from spending and delivery at any cost to spending and delivering at the right cost. We're moving towards a policy-first approach to many of our policy areas and... objectives. We're also creating a clearer business environment, one that aligns the regulatory environment in the Kingdom with international laws."

That includes the recent announcement of a 15% minimum effective tax rate on multinational profits, which Alibrahim said would "create a clearer environment for the private sector to operate," as the government looks to attract more external investment.

Saudi pulls back non-essential spending

Saudi Arabia has been on a mammoth capital spending spree since it launched its Vision 2030 plan to reduce its dependence on oil revenue in 2016, deploying the resources of its sovereign wealth fund — the Public Investment Fund, or PIF.

But more recently, it has reassessed the cost and commercial prospects of initiatives such as the new economic region NEOM and the futuristic "The Line" city, withdrawn funding from the LIV Golf tournament and halted construction on a planned giant skyscraper in Riyadh. In January, it said it would postpone hosting the 2029 Asian Winter Games, which had been scheduled for Trojena, a planned part of NEOM.

Saudi Arabia is meanwhile grappling with the destabilizing effects of ongoing strikes by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, which have hit targets including the PIF tower, Riyadh Airport and the country's largest oil refinery. The danger forced the Kingdom to call off its big international investor conference, dubbed "Davos in the Desert," which was due to be attended by some of the biggest figures in global finance in November.

"The human cost of crisis has been real, and so has been the economic cost," Alibrahim told CNBC.

Alibrahim said infrastructure investments had allowed the Kingdom's energy sector to restore production to near pre-crisis levels. It has meanwhile moved its import and export hub from the east to the west of the country via land-based transport due to the airport strikes, which has restored cargo levels.

He added that the attacks highlight the importance of diversification to the Saudi economy.

Real GDP contracted by 3.8% in the third quarter, according to government figures, with oil activities down 20.4% year-on-year partially offset by a 1.9% rise in non-oil activities. Net foreign direct investment inflows dropped 19.5% year-on-year in the second quarter.

The Saudi Ministry of Finance expects an overall contraction of around 2.1% this year and a rebound of 10.9% next year.

Advisory group Oxford Economics forecasts a more negative outlook. It sees the Saudi economy shrinking 3.4% this year and by 4% in 2027, amid escalating attacks on energy infrastructure even as a new minimum wage and continued Vision 2030 spending are expected to support incomes and domestic demand.

Akanksha Samdani, lead economist at Oxford Economics, said Vision 2030 was entering a new phase focused on returns.

"The government is managing fiscal pressures and shifting budgetary spending towards essential services and strategic priorities, while PIF is becoming more selective in its capital allocation and seeking greater private-sector participation," Samdani said, adding that some giga projects are being scaled back or delayed, while investment continues in sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, tourism, mining and technology.

"Our forecasts already assume that some of the Vision 2030 targets will be achieved later than originally planned. But the overarching goal of economic diversification remains unchanged," Samdani told CNBC by email.

Neil Quilliam, managing director of consultancy Azure Strategy, said investors are assessing whether Houthi attacks demonstrate a persistent vulnerability that could increase the cost and complexity of delivering Vision 2030.

"They have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to target important economic infrastructure and expose weaknesses in Saudi air defences," he told CNBC, with the attacks challenging the "assumption that Saudi Arabia has insulated itself from regional instability."

The economic impact of the strikes will be less about physical damage and more about whether they affect confidence in Saudi Arabia as a destination for tourism, entertainment and sports, a key part of Vision 2030 and a source of foreign capital and expatriate talent, he added.

One of the world's largest oil refineries is set to become Africa's biggest public firm in a highly anticipated offering that the continent's richest man has marketed as an "IPO for the people."

Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE, founded by Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, is expected to begin trading in Lagos on Dec. 1, according to multiple media reports, following regulatory approval. A Dangote Refinery spokesperson did not respond to a CNBC request for comment.

The IPO of a minority stake in the refinery has reportedly been heavily oversubscribed, with investors from 120 countries and all 54 African countries applying to buy shares, Dangote Refinery said. The shares were offered at 525 naira ($0.39).

Reuters' calculations put Dangote Refinery's IPO-implied valuation at about $47 billion, based on the offer price and the company's registered share count. That would make it the biggest stock market listing Africa has ever seen.

The Lagos-based refinery is regarded as a crown jewel of Nigeria's energy industry given the facility's role in transforming the oil-rich country's fuel market since it started operating in 2024.

"With a minimum subscription of just 10 shares, the offer is designed to give ordinary Nigerians and Africans an opportunity to own a stake in the refinery," Aliko Dangote said at the IPO launch in early September.

"The IPO is positioned not simply as a capital-raising exercise, but as an opportunity for workers, entrepreneurs and everyday Nigerians to participate in the refinery's future growth," he added.

Built for around $20 billion, the Dangote Refinery is now one of the largest in the world, with a crude oil distillation capacity of between 650,000 to 700,000 barrels per day.

It has emerged as a key provider of jet fuel in recent months, with buyers pivoting to West Africa amid Middle Eastern supply disruptions due to the Iran war.

"In theory, it's a win-win situation," Cyril Widdershoven, a maritime, energy and geopolitical analyst at Blue Water Strategy, told CNBC by phone.

Dangote Refinery has bolstered its reputation as a key Atlantic Basin facility amid soaring global demand for refined petroleum products, Widdershoven said, and the company intends to double its refining capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day by 2029, which could further strengthen its competitiveness in global markets.

However, despite the refinery's importance to Nigeria's economy, questions remain over its investment case, Widdershoven said, citing construction costs, commissioning delays, and the possibility that new capacity comes online with weaker margins.

"Right now it's like Anthropic or Nvidia, you are now buying the hype," Widdershoven said.

'An extremely strong year'

The Dangote Refinery has had "an extremely strong year," Mick Strautmann, market analyst at Vortexa, told CNBC by phone.

Between January and October, Vortexa data showed Dangote's seaborne refined product loadings stood at around 400,000 barrels per day, which is roughly 50% more than the same period last year.

More recently, however, the facility has seen refined-product loading jump to a record of 575,000 barrels per day through the first three weeks of November, surpassing an October record of 550,000 barrels per day, Strautmann said.

"It's been able to ramp up quite spectacularly and provide a lot of these products to the market in an extremely high price environment," Strautmann added.

"So, it's been one of the few places that's adding a lot of fuel supply to the Atlantic Basin, and at the same time, you know, to make West Africa less reliant on imports from other regions, particularly Europe for its gasoline supply," he said.

David Omojomolo, an emerging market economist focused on Africa at Capital Economics, said the upcoming Dangote Refinery IPO has captured global attention because the facility is seen as a rare example of an industrial policy success story on the African continent.

"It's been a good news story, and it's been an optimistic one as well," Omojomolo told CNBC.

"I don't want to be a hostage to fortune and say this time is different … but it does feel like a buzz and it's a question as to does it force other, say, billionaire industrialists to put their money where their mouth is in terms of helping the region's industrialisation prospects," he added.

In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jets emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.

Meanwhile, EHT observations in 2021 also resolved the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C 279 in unprecedented detail. These efforts, described in a paper that appeared in Astronomy & Astrophysics, revealed the jet's dynamics and geometry at subparsec scales, suggesting it bends toward Earth-based instruments on these scales. Combined with earlier EHT campaigns and multifrequency data, the EHT team's latest results are helping astronomers identify its nature and the mechanisms driving it.

By definition, blazars are bright galaxies with an SMBH at their centers—active galactic nuclei (AGNs)—that have relativistic jets of ionized matter directed straight toward Earth. Located approximately 538 million light-years away, 3C 279 has a central jet powered by an SMBH with an estimated mass of about 800 million solar masses (by comparison, Sagittarius A* is about 4.3 million solar masses). Because of its brightness, 3C 279 is considered a prime target for very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) and is frequently used for calibration.

The 2021 campaign represents the largest EHT array configuration published to date, with the addition of two new sites. These were the 12-m telescope at the Kitt Peak Observatory in Arizona and the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) interferometer in the French Alps. These additions provided crucial intermediate baselines that significantly improved coverage, especially at intermediate scales, enabling constraints on specific angular scales. These constraints were essential for probing both compact and extended structures in the jet.

Hendrik Müller, a staff scientist in the Data Management and Software (DMS) group at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) and a former researcher with the Max-Planck-Institut für Radioastronomie, was the lead author of the paper that appeared in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. As he told Universe Today via email, the EHT is continuously growing and adding more telescopes every year, including the Greenland Telescope in 2018. But as he noted, the Kitt Peak and NOEMA observatories were especially important to these observations:

The physical baseline between two antennas in the array determines the spatial scale that this baseline can resolve. That is, for example, the reason why the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is built on railway tracks: When you move the antennas closer to each other, you zoom out of the image and see the larger field of view.

If you move them closer to each other, you zoom into the image, achieve higher resolution, but see only a small view of the sky. The locations of the radio telescopes in the EHT could of course not be changed, but Kitt Peak and NOEMA were important because they are relatively close to other telescopes in the array (NOEMA in the French Alps to Pico Veleta close to Granada, Spain). They added information that was not available to us in previous years.

To process the volumes of data gathered by the EHT arrays, the team relied on Comrade, DoG-HiT, kine and Difmap imaging software, a strategy similar to the one used to reconstruct the famous M87 black hole image in 2019.

As Müller explained, the team used different software packages that make different assumptions about the image to build confidence in the result by checking for consistency across methods. Beyond imaging, many more collaborators and software packages were involved in early data-processing steps, like correlation or calibration.

The results, as noted, suggest that the jet curves so that one section of it points closer to Earth. While the jet is already oriented toward our instruments, Müller explained how this small change can have two visible effects:

Because the plasma is moving close to the speed of light, its radiation is concentrated in the direction it's traveling. When that direction lines up more closely with Earth, we see brighter emission. At the same time, features in the jet are moving more nearly straight toward us, so they can appear to move more slowly across the sky. Think of a car coming almost head-on: it can be moving fast while barely shifting left or right in your field of view.

That's what makes the bend a useful explanation for 3C 279. Farther along the inner jet, we see brighter emission and slower apparent motion. Both can result from a change in direction, even if the plasma keeps moving just as fast. That also means the brightest spot in the image can be downstream from the black hole, where the jet points most directly at us.

What's more, the EHT images show that the direction of the inner jet changes over time, providing clues as to what is driving the jet. Those are two aspects of cancer—how well people respond to chemotherapy, and how tumors metastasize—where there’s a lot of variability between patients. For instance, one of the aims is to cut down on the rounds of chemotherapy that patients need, as well as minimize side effects, by tailoring treatments more specifically.

They biopsy samples from real patients to grow mini tumors on chips, which are then stored in a portable, self-contained, lunchbox-sized lab sent to the ISS. Encapsulate researchers on the ground monitor the development of the cells from Earth via camera feeds and other monitoring instruments.

“The astronauts didn’t need to touch anything,” Encapsulate founder Armin Rad told Upward, the ISS lab magazine. “Honestly, they just plugged it in like a coffee machine.”

Encapsulate’s experiments are scheduled to run for three years, backed up by further research and development in labs still weighed down by Earth’s gravitational pull.

It’s not just cancer tumors that are being grown in space either. There’s growing interest in manufacturing cancer drugs there as well. Microgravity is again the reason, because the same lack of pressure and pull that helps tumors expand properly can also allow drug crystals to fully form.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, technical detail

Should space data centers run on solar panels, nuclear reactors or both?

The last few days we've been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently—maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution?

According to another paper from Turyshev, it all depends on the mission requirements.

One major problem with using solar panels for orbital data centers is the sun doesn't always shine in their orbit. During some seasons, each orbital pass will result in the satellite crossing through Earth's shadow for up to 21 minutes. And given that these data centers orbit around 15 times each day, that means in a 24-hour day, the satellite spends around 5 hours and 13 minutes in Earth's shadow.

To combat this problem, engineers turn to an obvious solution—batteries. But they are notorious for being heavy, and according to Turyshev's calculations, providing enough storage capacity to combat a 21-minute stretch with no power would require a 1 MW data center cluster to haul 6.46 metric tons (7.12 tons) of batteries into orbit. Combine that with the needed solar panels and radiators to get rid of waste heat as infrared light, and you end up with a total mass of 43 metric tons (47 tons) for a 1 MW cluster, even before counting any actual computing hardware.

A fission reactor would eliminate the need for solar wings, as well as batteries. However, it doesn't really deal well with the other physical constraint on these systems—waste heat. While it eliminates the heat generated by the solar panels themselves, it introduces another engineering problem—getting rid of the heat at two different temperatures.

Running a nuclear fission reactor at 25% efficiency (which is pretty standard for thermal electrical conversion) would produce about 3 megawatts of conversion waste heat for every 1 megawatt of energy generated, meaning a 1-megawatt computing cluster creates about 3 megawatts of waste heat from its power conversion machinery alone. This waste heat would be at around 700 kelvins—more than double the maximum temperature that processors in the data centers need to be kept below in order not to fry themselves.

While this higher-temperature heat can be radiated away with a relatively compact radiator, it would have to be separate from the thermal sinks cooling the processors below their 320 kelvins ideal temperature. Ultimately, a nuclear-powered cluster would only need around 6% less low-temperature radiator area than a fully solar-powered version.

Despite that, after adding all the mass of the reactor, radiation shielding, power converters and all the other necessary equipment to run a nuclear reactor, fission initially looks like a winner. Compared to today's standard solar panels, a compact fission reactor is around 10 metric tons (11 tons) lighter per megawatt. And since weight is money in space, that sounds like a win.

However, there are several caveats to that. First, lighter, next-generation solar arrays are coming along quickly, whose increased efficiency could eliminate nuclear's advantage entirely. Or the engineers could boost the satellite's orbit up to 1,450 kilometers (900 miles), where Earth's shadow problem completely goes away and the satellite can consistently bathe in sunlight—admittedly ignoring the potential space debris and trapped radiation problems this causes, as well as the need for higher-power communications equipment.

Nuclear suffers from another disadvantage—radiation. Data centers in space already suffer from stray cosmic rays flipping bits unexpectedly. Putting one next to an active nuclear reactor subjects it to random gamma rays and neutrons as well. While this could be lessened a bit by putting the reactor on a long boom—physically separating it from the server racks and placing a dense "shadow shield" near the reactor to block radiation from reaching the computers—that would require extra weight in the form of cabling and the boom itself, eliminating more of nuclear's original weight advantage.

Despite all these trade-offs, there does appear to be a situation where running a hybrid of both solar and nuclear is the best option. If a mission requires a data center to survive a 24-hour failure of its main power system while keeping 20% emergency power active for safe-mode operation, an 80/20 nuclear/solar split weighs in at around 36 metric tons (40 tons), around a third of the weight of either as a standalone option due to the weight of batteries needed to meet those mission requirements.

But to be clear, without that power maintenance constraint, either system in a standalone configuration wins out on weight.

Ultimately, Turyshev thinks the financial picture is dependent on the lifespan of the nuclear reactor. Another disadvantage of a nuclear-powered satellite is it can't just burn up in the atmosphere at the end of its life—it has to be boosted to a "graveyard" orbit at around 2,000 km (1,240 miles), where a spent reactor would stay indefinitely.

But if a reactor lasts 10 years, Turyshev calculates that it would save around $190 per kilowatt-year in launch costs, whereas if it lasts for only two years (as many experimental space-based reactors are designed to), then that flips to a $783 per kilowatt-year deficit.…

The sleepy sickness in Vilhelmina—100-year-old mystery investigated

Researchers at CEDAR have studied and perhaps found an important piece in understanding one of the biggest medicinal mysteries of our time: the Sleepy Sickness that swept over Europe in the early 1900´s. During the 1920's, Sweden was one of the hardest-hit countries in the world, with the highest number of reported cases in Västerbotten, and especially the inland community of Vilhelmina.

Lena Karlsson and Erling Häggström Gunfridsson are both researchers at the Centre of Demographic and Ageing Research (CEDAR). On Sept. 8, they published a research article titled "Encephalitis lethargica in Sweden, 1920–1930: national incidence and the 1921 outbreak in northern Sweden," a study that investigates the geographic spread of the mysterious sleepy sickness. The work is published in the journal Epidemiology and Infection.

Wanted to examine the spread in Sweden

The disease encephalitis lethargica, or sleepy sickness, emerged around 1926 and disappeared around 1930, and what caused this disease is a mystery to this day. Sweden was one of the hardest-hit countries, which made the researchers Lena and Erling interested in examining how the disease spread in the country. To map the spread, they analyzed national statistics from historical health care reports from SCB, and provincial medical reports from Regionarkivet Västerbotten.

"We wanted to see the geographic spread of the disease, and which other epidemics emerged before and after the outbreak. We also wanted to see if the results could contribute to understanding possible causes and mechanisms of the disease," says Karlsson.

The results show Vilhelmina as the hardest-hit community

The results show a clear geographical pattern in the spread of the sleepy sickness. It affected the Stockholm area first, and then quickly spread north. In 1921, Sweden had the highest number of reported cases in the world, with a concentration in Västerbotten. Out of all reported cases in Västerbotten, almost 80% were located in Vilhelmina. The result surprised the researchers, since epidemics usually hit the hardest in densely populated cities, rather than sparsely populated areas.

"We suspect that the sleepy sickness most likely spread in the cities first, but that it happened before it was mandatory to report the cases," explains Häggström Gunfridsson.

Can perhaps explain the development of the disease

Another interesting discovery was that Vilhelmina had severe cases of both the Spanish flu and mumps prior to the sleepy sickness outbreak, which may help explain the emergence of the sleepy sickness.

"We were surprised to find such a major mumps epidemic only a few months prior to the outbreak of the sleepy sickness. There are theories of a connection between the Spanish flu and sleepy sickness, but we could not see such connections in other areas. However, the combination of the Spanish flu and mumps may be relevant in the understanding of why Vilhelmina was so severely affected by the sleepy sickness. This finding is also consistent with hypotheses that multiple infections may have interacted in the development and spread of the disease," the researchers elaborate.

The results are relevant for the medical research of today

The study shows how important historical population and health data can be to reconstruct epidemics and thus highlight questions that are still relevant within medical research today. Additionally, the results can contribute new perspectives on post-infectious conditions and long-term effects after infections. These questions are still highly relevant to this day, for example when it comes to post-COVID.

Why it is here: useful update on pharmacy practices

Pharmacies get new powers to swap prescriptions during shortages

Pharmacies are being given more freedom over the prescription medicines they can give to patients when items are out of stock.

Staff will be able to offer the same drug in a different strength or form â two 5mg tablets in the place of a 10mg pill, or a cream instead of an ointment, for example.

The change should help patients avoid repeat trips to their GP for an alternative prescription when the issue can be resolved safely and easily at the chemist.

And for the first time, children in England who miss their flu vaccination at school will be able to receive it at a pharmacy instead.

What can be swapped?

For decades, pharmacists have usually had to provide exactly the medicine prescribed by a doctor under rules set out in the 1968 Medicines Act.

If a product was out of stock, patients often had to return to their GP for an alternative prescription or wait for new supplies to arrive, if it was safe to do so.

Now, pharmacists will be able to make some tweaks without sending patients back to the doctor, including:

- supplying the same dose of a drug in different strength pills

- supplying the same medicine in a different form, such as a capsule rather than a solid tablet

The changes will apply across the UK once they have been approved by the relevant parliaments and assemblies.

Public health minister Diana Johnson said the new flexibility would make life easier for patients.

"When you go to the pharmacy to pick up your prescription, there is nothing worse than being told you need to contact your GP again because the exact medicine they've prescribed isn't available at that time, or in that form," she said.

"That's why we're changing the rules so that people can get the treatment they need with less hassle, and no delay."

Pharmacy expansion drive

The move follows a broader expansion of pharmacy services in England, which has given pharmacists greater powers to prescribe certain medications themselves without patients needing to see a GP at all.

That scheme now covers 12 common conditions:

- migraines

- acne

- scabies

- ear infections

- badly blocked noses

- sore throats

- earache

- sinusitis

- shingles

- impetigo

- infected bites

- urinary tract infections

Many other medicines, like certain painkillers and cold remedies, can also be bought over the counter at pharmacies without a prescription.

'Endemic' shortages

Henry Gregg from the National Pharmacy Association welcomed the move, but called for more action on drug shortages which he said were becoming endemic.

"These measures are a step forward but do not fix the underlying causes of shortages," he added.

"It's clear the government undervalues medicines, including underfunding vital local pharmacies.

"It must take action so that manufacturers don't favour other countries when stocks are low internationally."

The changes are separate from existing powers used during widespread medicine shortages.

If the government is concerned about national stocks of a particular medicine or medical product, it can still issue a Serious Shortage Protocol, external.

The measure has previously been used during shortages of some hormone replacement therapy (HRT) products, for example.

In those circumstances, pharmacists can already dispense an alternative without having to contact a GP first.

Should I get a flu vaccine now?

Health officials are urging more people to take up the offer of a free flu vaccine as the number of hospital patients seriously ill with the virus has risen sharply in the past week.

The flu surge has come slightly early this year but that is not completely unusual.

Flu activity is still at "moderate levels" and the peak may not arrive until December or early January, health officials warn.

So what is the advice on getting a vaccine, who can get it for free and who should pay?

How effective is the flu vaccine?

"If you're offered it, it's a good idea to have it," says Prof Nick Hopkinson, professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London.

"The main reason is to avoid serious complications in vulnerable groups â so as many as possible should have it in those groups.

"People don't understand it's a potentially life-threatening infection and that the vaccine is safe."

Flu is a viral infection which affects the nose, throat and lungs. Often it goes away on its own but it can make people seriously ill â complications can include pneumonia, heart attacks and other underlying illnesses getting worse.

It can also kill.

In England last winter, UKHSA estimated there were 3,798 deaths attributed to influenza.

Scientists have to predict which strains of influenza will be circulating before the vaccine is manufactured each year in time for winter.

The current one protects against three strains â two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain.

Even if these strains drift slightly, experts say getting vaccinated is still a good idea to lower the risk of severe illness.

Who is currently missing out?

Millions of vulnerable people are eligible for the free jab to help protect them against flu, including children, pregnant women, care home residents, people with lung conditions and anyone aged 65 and over.

But only around a third of under-65s and two-thirds of those aged 65 and over have been vaccinated so far this winter.

That leaves around seven million people unprotected at present, health officials say.

Parents are being urged to vaccinate young children in order to protect them and other people they come into contact with.

Can I still get flu if I've been vaccinated?

Yes. The vaccine does not rule out the possibility you will get flu, but it does reduce the chances you'll become very ill with it and end up in hospital.

It takes two weeks for your body's immunity to build up after being vaccinated, which is another reason to have the jab sooner rather than later.

Protection from the vaccine reduces the risk of serious flu complications by 50%, says Prof Hopkinson.

If I'm young and healthy, do I need it?

If you are not eligible for the free flu vaccine, you can still buy it from most pharmacies for between Â£15 and 25.

"It's a reasonable thing to consider," says Prof Hopkinson.

But it is far more important for the millions of vulnerable people offered it free to be vaccinated.

They are known to be at risk of health complications from the virus.

Other groups are also at risk: "Smokers are five times more likely to get flu â so quit now," he suggests.

Am I depriving someone else if I buy the jab?

Simply put, no.

There are different vaccines for those getting it free on the NHS and those paying for it privately.

However, the vaccines do the same job and protect against the same strains of flu.

Pharmacist Olivier Picard says he's seen a "massive spike in demand" for flu jabs in the last 24 hours.

Most "paste your text, get a PDF" tools upload your document to a server. That means your notes, contracts, or drafts sit in someone else's queue and probably in their logs.

MarkPDF Lite takes the opposite approach: the entire conversion pipeline runs in your browser tab. Zero uploads, zero tracking, zero server.

How it works

The whole app is 4 static files (HTML + CSS + a small script) hosted on GitHub Pages. Two CDN libraries do the heavy lifting:

- markdown-it parses your Markdown into HTML locally:

const md = window.markdownit({

html: false, // raw HTML is escaped, not injected

linkify: true, // bare URLs become clickable

breaks: true // single newlines render as <br>

});

function render() {

docEl.innerHTML = md.render(mdEl.value);

- html: false means user input is treated as Markdown, never as executable HTML. No XSS surface from the editor itself.

item.title: Swap the Coding-Agent Plugin. Recheck the Boundary.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Swap the Coding-Agent Plugin. Recheck the Boundary.

“We approved that coding agent” stops being a useful sentence when someone replaces the agent underneath it.

Same terminal. Same project. A different set of tools, plugins or execution paths. The approval may now describe a configuration nobody is running.

Extensibility lets a team reuse its own agent, change its workspace and keep the interface it likes. Each swap also needs a specific answer: which assumptions did this change invalidate?

The plugin menu isn't the execution boundary

Pax makes this concrete. Its coding agent is replaceable, plugins extend its capabilities, and workspaces determine where workspace-backed file and shell operations run.

There are three surfaces to keep separate:

- The tools exposed to the model: what it can request.

- The workspace used by file and shell tools: where those operations execute.

- The Python plugin code: what runs with the host user's authority.

Pax's documented default runs commands and edits files as the user, without a sandbox or approval step. That is a default to account for, not a newly discovered vulnerability or a description of every custom setup.

Routing workspace-backed tools into a sandbox changes an important execution path. It does not, by itself, establish that arbitrary plugin code is contained there too. The plugin trust warning concerns that separate host-side execution.

A sandbox-backed shell and an unreviewed host plugin can coexist. Inspect both.

Replacing the agent is different from extending it

With --agent, Pax loads the supplied agent without Pax's plugins. You get your agent's tools and instructions, not the default composition with a different name attached.

That can be exactly what you want: develop an agent in your codebase and use it through a terminal without rewriting its behavior for the interface.

It also makes inherited assumptions dangerous. If a safeguard came from a default plugin, don't assume it survives the replacement. Conversely, loading a custom agent doesn't prove safeguards are missing; the replacement may supply its own.

Inventory the actual composition. A “reviewer” with file-editing and shell tools is not read-only because its name sounds cautious.

Reopen the checks the change actually affects

A different color scheme doesn't need a security audit. A new Python plugin deserves more scrutiny than a UI preference.

Here's a proposed change-impact matrix:

The folder-trust distinction is especially easy to miss. In Pax, an untrusted folder still allows reading, editing and code execution. The trust setting affects instruction treatment; it isn't a read-only switch.

Instruction handling also changes across versions. Pydantic AI v2.75.0 changed how RepoContext, Skills and Memory present workspace text below operator authority. That is relevant to a configuration review, but it isn't OS isolation.

Record the version you evaluated. A remembered UI label cannot tell you which instruction rules or tool composition are active today.

Keep a before-and-after record

Consider a hypothetical team replacing its default coding agent with a project-specific reviewer while retaining a sandbox-backed workspace.

Use this proposed record to capture the change. Its values and results are intentionally unfilled: it isn't a Pax configuration format, and no checks were executed for this article.

“Same workspace” is useful information, but insufficient. A replacement tool might perform its work outside that workspace abstraction. A new hook might execute host code before any model-requested shell command.

Changed fields reopen the affected checks. Unchanged fields preserve context, not a guarantee of safety. Keep the record small enough to update alongside the configuration change.

Check denied actions, not just useful ones

Use synthetic data in a disposable evaluation environment. Define the restrictions before running candidate code, including the host-side paths you intend to constrain.

First, check an intended action: can the configured tool edit the designated fixture file?

Then check the boundary: attempt access to an out-of-scope fixture and a controlled network destination outside the allowlist. Require denial from enforced policy. A model politely declining a request is not the same result.

Finally, inspect host-side plugin and hook paths. Test the relevant ones under the intended restrictions; a passing workspace-tool check doesn't cover code that bypasses that tool.

These are proposed checks, not completed results or sandbox certification. Record what was exercised, what denied the action and what remains untested. If the promised restriction cannot be enforced, don't approve that configuration for the workload.

The next time someone swaps a plugin, the useful question isn't whether the team still trusts Pax. It's whether the changed configuration still has evidence for the boundary the team relies on.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

ALTER TABLE ... Two bypasses sit outside the policy list, so a policy-by-policy review never sees them.

1. The table owner is not subject to RLS

relrowsecurity = true only means the table participates in RLS. Unless relforcerowsecurity is also true, the table owner bypasses the policies. If a migration, a helper job or an old service account owns your tables, "RLS is on" is a misleading status line.

select c.relname, c.relrowsecurity, c.relforcerowsecurity, r.rolname as owner,

r.rolsuper, r.rolbypassrls

from pg_class c

join pg_roles r on r.oid = c.relowner

where c.relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace and c.relkind = 'r';

Do not flip FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY blindly: the owner is then subject to the policies too, and a too-narrow policy set can break legitimate writes. Check the owner first, then decide between FORCE and re-owning the table with a low-privilege role.

2. SECURITY DEFINER functions and unpinned search_path

A definer function runs with its owner's privileges. If that owner is privileged, and anon can EXECUTE it, an attacker gets owner-level behaviour without touching any table policy. An unpinned search_path adds a second problem: resolution can be steered at call time.

select p.proname, p.prosecdef, r.rolname as owner,

r.rolsuper, r.rolbypassrls,

p.proconfig as pinned_settings,

pg_get_function_identity_arguments(p.oid) as args

from pg_proc p

join pg_roles r on r.oid = p.proowner

where p.pronamespace = 'public'::regnamespace

and p.prosecdef = true

order by p.proname;

Fix direction: set search_path = '' in the function definition, validate auth.uid() inside the function, and REVOKE EXECUTE ... FROM anon unless the endpoint is genuinely public.

A composition trap worth knowing

Permissive policies combine with OR, restrictive ones with AND. pg_policies.permissive stores the full strings PERMISSIVE / RESTRICTIVE — not single letters. A checker that looks for P / R substrings silently skips every row, then reports "no findings". That is why I also persist a fingerprint of the objects actually scanned (object names plus a catalog snapshot hash) and refuse to overwrite a baseline on an empty or malformed scan. First run = baseline; later runs = new and resolved findings only.

The ten read-only catalog checks behind that baseline are in a free nightly n8n drift monitor — it queries only pg_catalog, pg_policies, pg_roles and information_schema, reads no application rows and writes nothing.

Honest limit: catalog drift is not an exploit test. A clean diff means the checked catalog shapes did not change; it is not proof that no data is reachable.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

How gamers are using AI and leaked files to clone Grand Theft Auto 6

Hot off its record-breaking console launch, the developer of Grand Theft Auto 6 is facing a problem â and it's one that is increasingly affecting the wider games industry.

Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6, but with the emergence of powerful AI tools, coders and gamers have taken matters into their own hands.

The developer has typically released Grand Theft Auto on PC long after its initial console launch â 19 months later in the case of GTA 5.

This time it may not have that luxury â in part because of an apparent leak of files from an Xbox development build of the game, but also due to the rapid advance of AI coding platforms.

These tools are being used to recreate or adapt existing games, sometimes within days, taking away the control developers have over their products.

Barely a week after the release of GTA 6, efforts are already under way to get an unofficial version playable on PC, although some projects have faced takedown notices from the game's publisher.

For some gamers, it's an exciting prospect, despite the legal questions surrounding the process.

For developers, it may be a warning: if a game as big as GTA 6 can be recreated, what does that mean for everyone else?

Like 'looking at a painting and making your own replica'

The recent wave of AI-assisted game recreation has been widely linked to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model, released in September, and to agentic tools such as Claude Code.

Mark Brown, creator of the YouTube channel Game Maker's Toolkit and whose own game Word Play was recently recreated using AI, said cloning largely took two forms: replication and reverse engineering.

Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game based on an existing one, possibly using screenshots or a description.

This, he said, was similar to "looking at a painting and making your own replica" â something which is "a very close copy, but is ultimately a new painting".

It's a particular issue among smaller studios, many of whom worry that AI makes it easier for others to copy their work.

When indie developers Sodoj and Marco from the studio Robotonic noticed a version of their unreleased puzzle game 204Snake appear on the free games platform Yandex with the same name, they were "appalled".

"The game was essentially the exact same idea, the exact same mechanics as we had, but with the art looking a bit off," Marco told the BBC.

The duo were able to issue a copyright strike to Yandex and Google to get the copy taken down, but said it only felt like a "small victory".

The second approach â reverse engineering â involves working backwards from a finished game to understand how it was created.

One way of doing this is decompilation, which attempts to turn the game's final version into something closer to its original source code.

Brown compares the process to "taking a cake and somehow turning it back into the original recipe, with the exact quantities of flour, eggs, and milk used, so anyone can remake the same cake".

Reverse-engineering projects have helped bring games such as Halo: Combat Evolved and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsers.

A related technique, recompilation, can help adapt a game that has been reverse-engineered to run on different hardware. This is one of the methods being explored in efforts to get GTA 6 onto PC.

Coders wanting to attempt this with Rockstar's latest game face a difficult task because of its sheer size and complexity.

Earlier in November, Cyberleek â a hacker or group of hackers â released what they claimed to be a near-complete Xbox development build of the game. They later leaked what they claimed to be the missing .exe file needed to launch the game.

It gave those working on an unofficial PC version a crucial new starting point.

"Now people are using AI to try and decompile it, make a modified version that could run on PC, and compile a new version," said Brown.

Since the leak, several groups have posted claims of their progress on platforms such as X, ranging from getting the game to boot up to making it run at a stable rate.

One attempt seen by the BBC on X purported to have some of the game running nearly as smoothly as it does on console, albeit on a high-end PC.

Accounts and sites have even sprung up to track the various attempts, excitedly sharing clips of the latest milestone passed and scoring their efforts.

Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, have not confirmed the authenticity of the leaked build, and neither has responded to the BBC's request for a statement.

However, Take-Two has issued take, externaldown notices, external of public projects aiming to port the Xbox version to PC on platforms such as GitHub.

"There are no remedies available to rectify this clear attempt to facilitate copyright infringement based upon Take-Two's copyrighted property," one notice stated.

Tech Life: One hundred years of AI

Laura Cress talks to game designers who say their unreleased new game was copied using AI. And Shiona McCallum reports on a new AI police chatbot.

Available for over a year

Why is there a wait for the official PC version?

News of the leak has been celebrated by some gamers on Reddit, who resent having to wait for the PC release.

"Why should the PC players have to wait half a year if you can develop the game in weeks as shown so far!" wrote one gamer, external.

"Will be funny when the decomp runs way better than whatever Rockstar can make," said another.

Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, said part of the reason why the games are often released on PCs months after consoles is that PC versions are "complex" with "different hardware configurations", as opposed to the more standardised set-up of consoles.

He added there could also be a more commercial reason, as Rockstar can "have a second moment when the PC version is ready".…

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Key Takeaways

- Smartphone GPS, motion sensors, and vehicle interfaces can each report valid measurements that produce incorrect results when combined without accounting for timing and coordinate frames.

- Preserve raw observations and their provenance before synchronizing, transforming, or normalizing them.

- Introduce a quality gate that determines whether telemetry is suitable for a particular decision instead of forcing every observation into a definitive result.

- Design for real-world conditions, including delayed GPS updates, phone movement, background interruptions, and intermittent connectivity.

- Monitor data quality alongside conventional application and infrastructure metrics because a functioning pipeline can still produce unreliable driving events.

Why this matters: the phone is not the vehicle

A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.

Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.

However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.

In fact, a GPS update may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.

Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.

I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.

This distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.

Who should read this, and what will they gain?

For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.

For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.

For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.

For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.

The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.

How this architecture took shape

I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.

This led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.

Start with the architecture, not the algorithm

I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.

A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image shows. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.

A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.

item.title: India uses $1.62 billion in Nepal aid to lock in regional influence—and perhaps ward off China, analysts say
item.description:
