India announced a $1.62 billion economic package for flood-hit Nepal on Nov. 23, pairing reconstruction grants with a credit line for energy projects, the latest move in a decades-old contest with China over the Himalayan country’s future.

The floods that hit Nepal in late August were among the worst disasters in the country’s recorded history, killing at least 1,300 people. An estimated 84,270 people, including over 32,000 children, were affected by the floods, according to UNICEF.

“It has been three months and families are still working hard to rebuild, but efforts are hampered by the loss of assets and livelihoods they depend on,” Andrea Berardo, the World Food Programme’s deputy country director in Nepal, said in a Nov. 24 statement. “With winter approaching in Nepal’s highlands, many families are still living in temporary shelters and are facing increasingly harsh conditions.”

The money is about more than rebuilding damaged roads and homes. India—already Nepal’s largest trading partner—is using disaster aid to reinforce its ties with a neighbor that China has courted for years, and to keep Nepal’s economic future closely linked to its own, analysts say.

What’s in the package?

India’s package to Nepal includes a $377 million grant for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure projects, along with a $1.24 billion line of credit for energy projects, according to a joint statement by the two countries.

Nepal is likely to use the grant for reconstruction and the credit line—which carries preferential terms and sourcing requirements from India—for infrastructure, notes Constantino Xavier, a nonresident fellow at the Brookings Institution’s foreign policy program. The credit line could also foster cross-border supply chains and support Nepal’s industrialization and manufacturing ambitions, which are essential to creating jobs in one of Asia’s youngest countries.

The announcement followed talks in New Delhi between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah. It was the first official bilateral trip abroad for the 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician since he took office in March, after 2025’s youth-led protests against corruption.

“Our commitment will be to help affected families get their lives back on track, create new opportunities and further strengthen Nepal’s capacity to deal with future disasters,” Modi said to reporters.

Shah thanked India for consistently acting as a first responder to Nepal during “times of natural disasters and difficult hours”, and invited Modi to visit Nepal. India was the first foreign government to respond to the August floods, sending relief supplies and helping restore communications.

A Post-Disaster Needs Assessment released this month by Nepal’s National Planning Commission estimates recovery and reconstruction will cost 706.65 billion Nepali rupees ($5.2 billion)—more than 10% of Nepal’s 2025 GDP of $45.49 billion, according to the World Bank.

Has India done this before?

India and Nepal have maintained close economic, diplomatic and security ties since they signed the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship; bilateral trade reached $9.38 billion in the 2025–26 fiscal year.

After a 2015 earthquake in Nepal that killed more than 8,000 people, India donated $1 billion for post-earthquake reconstruction. Yet five months later, many Nepalis blamed India for a fuel shortage, accusing New Delhi of imposing an undeclared blockade after Nepal adopted a new constitution. India denied responsibility, saying protests on the Nepali side of the border were blocking its trucks.

India has long used money to play a central role in South Asia. It provided nearly $4 billion in aid to Sri Lanka in 2022, as the tourism-dependent island nation faced its worst economic crisis in more than seven decades.

“It reflects India’s growing geoeconomic engagement with its neighbors, especially in times of crises, as also during Sri Lanka’s 2022 financial default,” Xavier says of the Nepal pledge.

There may also be a geopolitical motivation behind India’s generosity. Kunda Dixit, former editor of the Nepali Times, told Reuters that India “may be trying to ensure that [Shah] does not lean too much towards China.”

What about China?

China and Nepal share an 878-mile border across the Himalayas. China accounts for nearly half of Nepal’s foreign direct investment and is the country’s second-largest trading partner, though trade is heavily skewed in Beijing’s favor.

Beijing has also identified 10 projects for potential joint implementation under its Belt and Road Initiative, including a proposed railway linking Kathmandu with Tibet, road corridors and a cross-border electricity transmission line. China also responded to the floods by providing cash and relief supplies, and sending more than 20 rescue and forensic experts.

In Nepal, India disbursed more than four times as much aid as China in the 2024–25 fiscal year, according to Nepali government data cited by Reuters.

“I don’t think China will launch a checkbook competition with India in Nepal,” Yun Sun, a senior fellow and co-director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, says. “Influence and presence are measured by long-term, consistent involvement, not a one-time deal. The region would benefit from contributions from all great powers, instead of a single package.”

“Many of the smaller South Asian states, including Nepal, rely substantively on India for development and humanitarian assistance,” Michael Kugelman, a resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, says. “India’s new aid package is the latest reminder that even with China deepening its footprint in South Asia, New Delhi continues to leverage reliance on its largesse to ensure ties with its neighbors—or at least most of them—remain in a good place.”

Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend.

Around 44% of employers plan to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report. About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases.

Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the new compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers.

“Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where inflation is a big concern.”

Dwindling pay budgets and flat raises amid economic uncertainty

Job seekers and staffers alike are suffering through a difficult labor market: Hiring has slowed, layoffs are steadily streaming in, and wages don’t feel like they’re holding up. Looking at the year ahead, the picture doesn’t look too pretty.

Wall Street analysts and business executives have been floating the idea we’re in a “K-shaped economy”; higher-income Americans are witnessing their earnings and wealth rise, while lower-income people are struggling against smaller gains and the high cost of living. The concept has come to explain the confusing U.S. economy, where solid overall growth contrasts with sluggish hiring and rising unemployment.

While U.S. companies are holding their average salary increase budget steady at 3.5%, according to a 2025 report from Willis Towers Watson, there’s a large cohort that is planning to scale back. Nearly a third of businesses plan to lower their compensation-increase budgets compared to last year, citing a potential recession, dwindling financial performance, and desire for more control over costs.

Last year, one high-profile employer ditched its merit-based raises in favor of a general, flat pay bump. Starbucks announced it would be giving a standard 2% raise to all salaried North American employees in 2025, diverging from the norm that managers have a say in the raises of their direct reports. It was all a part of CEO Brian Niccol’s bid to reduce costs in a broader company turnaround effort.

But Starbucks is just one notable name in a growing list of employers hunkering down for economic hardship. Lexi Clarke, Payscale’s chief people officer, told Fortune last year that pay-increase budgets are being slimmed as tariffs and economic woes create uncertainty, forcing many employers to be on their guard.

“Economic concerns have now overtaken labor competition as the primary driver of compensation decisions,” Clarke said, as “66% of employers cite this as the reason for pulling back, up 17% from last year.”

As more companies trim back wage budgets and hand out peanut butter raises, there are many still reinvesting in their star talent. America’s largest private employer, $988 billion retail titan Walmart, unrolled a strategy in 2024 to pay its top store managers up to $620,000 per year.

Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback. The shares jumped about 30% on the news. The founder was back at his desk. Order restored.

I read it differently. Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it. The board failed that test, and the way it failed should worry directors at every company whose CEO looks irreplaceable.

The sequence of events tells a story.

On November 12, Nvidia announced that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation, after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The board said it would consider internal and external candidates.

Five days later, on the earnings call, chair Harvey Jones told analysts the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen.”

Then the alternatives fell away. The Financial Times reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, the Arm CEO who spent seven years at Nvidia. On November 23, Haas extended his contract at Arm through 2033. The same day, Nvidia’s directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, saying they had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government. Trump told CNBC that he made a personal assurance that sealed the decision.

The board’s own independent investigation is still open. The directors reinstated their CEO before their own inquiry had finished.

That’s the detail I can’t get past. A board that says no on a Tuesday and yes six days later has run out of options.

A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse.

Accountability depends on a credible alternative. When a board has a successor ready, its questions carry weight, because everyone in the room knows the company survives if the answers fall short. When it has nobody, the CEO holds the leverage and both sides know it. The duty to oversee him turns into a duty to keep him.

Huang has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993. The board had three decades to prepare for the day he wasn’t there. When that day came, it had a CFO doing two jobs, one outside name, and a market that wanted him back. Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld wrote in Fortune the board had no Plan B.

Investors made the same point from the other side. Within days of the resignation, prominent shareholders were urging the board to keep the door open to Huang. Nobody outside the company had the facts. What they were pricing was a business with no one else to run it.

The board has since created a national security committee and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Those are controls on conduct. Neither one is a successor.

I coach CEOs, and I’ve watched how boards arrive here. Nobody decides to skip succession. It gets postponed, one good quarter at a time.

Over the years a founder’s identity and the company’s fuse. Raising the question of who comes next starts to feel like disloyalty, so directors leave it for another meeting. The CEO rarely pushes either. Planning your own exit means picturing a company that no longer needs you, and that is the hardest thing to ask of someone whose whole identity is the company.

So both sides stay comfortable. The cost arrives on the one day the board needs a choice and finds it doesn’t have one.

Plenty of boards are living with the same arrangement right now, and it’s invisible for as long as the results are good.

Two tests will tell a director where their board stands.

First, name the person who could run the company on Monday. One name, already inside the building, whom the top team would follow. If the honest answer is the CFO as caretaker, you have a holding pattern.

Second, recall the last time the board said no to the CEO on something he cared about. If nobody can remember one, the board has already stopped overseeing him. It just hasn’t been tested yet.

Huang may prove to be the right leader for Nvidia’s next chapter. The investigation may answer every open question. Neither would change what the 11 days showed.

The board now enters the next crisis in a weaker position than the last one. It has shown its investors, its government and its CEO that it has no alternative to him. He knows it. So does everyone who will ever need to challenge him.

Every director reading this should ask the question Nvidia’s board had to answer in public.

If our CEO were gone tomorrow, would we have a choice?

“The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.”

The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department.

The BEA operates with statistical and methodological independence, a safeguard designed to protect the accuracy and impartiality of its statistics.

On Wednesday, the BEA issued revisions to its growth figures for the third quarter of 2026, saying GDP was 4.3%—not the 3.9% it had originally forecast. The upward revision of 0.9% on the initial estimate was “primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending.”

Analysts are unlikely to be surprised. Revisions are a routine feature of U.S. economic statistics. Lower survey response rates have reduced the precision of some estimates. As UBS’s Pauk Donovan said in a note to clients this morning: “Changes in U.S. economic growth are exaggerated by the fiction of annualization (a technique employed by very few advanced economies).”

Ferrero Rocher Blossom Cookies

Chocolate hazelnut lovers, these Ferrero Rocher blossom cookies are for you! They take classic thumbprint cookies to a whole new level of flavor and texture.

Chocolate-hazelnut lovers, you might want to sit down for this one. These Ferrero Rocher blossom cookies aren’t your average thumbprint cookies. We’re talking rich chocolate cookies rolled in crunchy chopped hazelnuts, filled with a gooey dollop of Nutella and finished with an entire Ferrero Rocher chocolate perched on top. They’re a little over the top in the very best way.

Every bite is a delicious mix of soft, crunchy, creamy, chocolatey and nutty. They’re almost too pretty to eat (almost!), and they’re guaranteed to steal the show at a holiday cookie exchange. They make a pretty impressive homemade gift, too. Just be prepared for everyone to ask for the recipe.

Ingredients for Ferrero Rocher Blossom Cookies

- Butter: Start with softened butter so it creams easily with the sugar. And don’t skimp on the creaming time! Beating the butter and sugar for at least five minutes incorporates tiny air pockets into the dough, resulting in light, tender cookies.

- Sugar: Granulated white sugar sweetens the cookie dough and crisps up the cookie edges.

- Egg: You’ll need to separate an egg for these cookies. The yolk adds richness and tenderness to the cookie dough, while the white helps the chopped hazelnuts stick to the outside. Let the egg come to room temperature before starting so it blends easily into the dough.

- Milk: A splash of milk adds moisture and brings the chocolate cookie dough together. Any kind of milk you have in the fridge will work.

- Vanilla: A little vanilla extract enhances the chocolate and hazelnut flavors.

- Flour: Nothing fancy needed here! Be sure to spoon regular all-purpose flour into your measuring cup and level it off rather than scooping straight from the bag.

- Baking cocoa: This is what gives the cookies their rich chocolate flavor! Reach for unsweetened cocoa powder, not hot chocolate mix, which has added sugar and other ingredients.

- Hazelnuts: Toast the hazelnuts before chopping them to bring out their flavor, then let them cool completely before rolling the cookie dough balls in them.

- Chocolate hazelnut spread: Nutella is the classic choice, but any chocolate-hazelnut spread will work. It creates a slightly gooey filling in the center of each cookie, and acts as the glue that holds the chocolate candy in place.

- Ferrero Rocher chocolates: These individually wrapped chocolate-hazelnut candies are the finishing touch. Each one is a whole hazelnut enrobed in creamy filling and a crisp chocolate-and-hazelnut shell. Unwrap the candies before the cookies come out of the oven so they’re ready to be pressed into the warm centers.

Directions

Step 1: Make the cookie dough

In a large bowl, cream the butter and sugar with a handheld mixer until they’re light and fluffy, five to seven minutes. Beat in the egg yolk, milk and vanilla.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, cocoa powder and salt. Gradually add the dry ingredients to the creamed mixture, mixing until a soft dough forms. Cover and refrigerate the dough for about one hour, or until it’s firm enough to handle.

Editor’s Tip: Don’t skip chilling the dough. It makes it easier to roll into balls and helps the cookies hold their shape as they bake.

Step 2: Shape the cookies

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a small bowl, whisk the egg white until it’s foamy. Shape the chilled dough into 1-1/2-inch balls. Dip the balls into the egg white, letting any excess drip off, then roll them in the chopped hazelnuts to coat.

Arrange the dough balls on greased baking sheets. Use the end of a wooden spoon handle to gently press an indentation into the center of each cookie.

Step 3: Bake the cookies

Bake the cookies for 13 to 15 minutes, or until the centers of the cookies are set.

Step 4: Fill the cookies

While the cookies are still warm, spoon or pipe a small dollop of Nutella into each indentation. Gently press an unwrapped Ferrero Rocher chocolate into the center of each cookie.

Carefully transfer the cookies from the baking sheets to wire racks to cool completely.

Editor’s Tip: A piping bag or small zip-top bag with one corner snipped off makes it easy to add the Nutella neatly to the centers.

Recipe Variations

- Switch up the nuts: No hazelnuts in the pantry? Finely chopped almonds, pecans or walnuts all make a delicious crunchy coating. You can also skip the nuts and roll the dough balls in granulated sugar instead.

- Try a different filling: Replace the regular chocolate-hazelnut spread with Nutella Peanut, plain peanut butter, cookie butter or another chocolaty spread. Just keep in mind that swapping the filling will change the flavor of the finished cookies.

- Add a flavor boost: Stir 1 teaspoon of instant espresso powder—the secret ingredient for better chocolate treats—into the dry ingredients to deepen the chocolate flavor without making the cookies taste like coffee.

- Swap the candy: Instead of Ferrero Rocher chocolates, press a chocolate kiss, chocolate truffle or mini peanut butter cup into the warm cookies. It’s an easy way to make several varieties from one batch of dough.

How to Store Ferrero Rocher Blossom Cookies

Let the cookies cool completely, then transfer them to an airtight cookie storage container. Store them at room temperature in a cool, dry place for up to five days. If you need to stack them, place a sheet of parchment or wax paper between layers to protect the chocolate toppings.

Can you make chocolate hazelnut cookies ahead of time?

Absolutely! These cookies stay fresh for several days when stored properly, so you can bake them a day or two before serving.

You can also prepare the cookie dough up to two days in advance and keep it covered in the refrigerator. When you’re ready to bake, let the dough sit at room temperature for a few minutes, then shape, coat and bake the cookies as directed.…

Mistletoe Martini

A mistletoe martini is holiday sparkle you can sip. It tastes like a frosty-cold vodka-cranberry with added floral notes, and the most festive garnish you can dream of.

The mistletoe martini is the perfect spirited sipper for your holiday parties. It’s flavored with cranberry—a classic December flavor—but adds elderflower liqueur and a little simple syrup for a French kiss of floral sweetness. A hard shake turns the concoction into a cocktail that feels way fancier than the effort it takes.

You don’t have to be a bartender or jolly old St. Nick to whip one up. The hardest part is the garnish, and even that is just a couple of sage leaves cozied up between two cranberries on a pick. Just don’t garnish it with actual mistletoe, no matter how hard you’re angling for a smooch, because mistletoe is toxic. Let it work its magic from the doorway, not your glass! Shake up a mistletoe martini for yourself after a long night of gift wrapping, or batch a pitcher and make it the most kissable drink in your lineup of Christmas cocktails.

Mistletoe Martini Ingredients

- Cranberry juice: Cranberry juice gives this cocktail its festive ruby color and the tart backbone that keeps it from tasting like candy.

- Vodka: Vodka is the clean, neutral base that lets the cranberry and elderflower do the talking. A good mid-range bottle you’d happily sip is perfect, so save the top-shelf vodka brand for a classic martini.

- Elderflower liqueur: This French liqueur is made from elderflower blossoms, and tastes floral and lightly sweet with notes of pear, lychee and citrus. A few well-known brands include St-Germain, St. Elder and Giffard.

- Simple syrup: Simple syrup is just sugar dissolved in water. It balances the tart cranberry juice. You can buy it bottled, but it takes about five minutes to prep homemade simple syrup.

- Sage leaves: Fresh sage adds a woodsy, savory aroma, and its soft green color looks gorgeous against the red drink. Choose bright, perky leaves without any brown spots or wilting.

- Cranberries: Fresh cranberries skewered on a pick turn this drink into a tiny holiday decoration.

Directions

Step 1: Fill the shaker

Fill a shaker with ice.

Step 2: Add the ingredients

Add the vodka, cranberry juice, elderflower liqueur and simple syrup.

Editor’s Tip: If you’re not sure how sweet your cranberry juice is, start with half the simple syrup and add more to taste.

Step 3: Shake the cocktail

Shake hard until the liquid is very cold and the shaker is frosty, about 10 to 15 seconds.

Step 4: Strain the cocktail over fresh ice

Strain the cocktail and pour it over fresh ice into a cocktail glass.

Editor’s Tip: Pop your glasses in the freezer for 10 to 15 minutes before guests arrive so they stay frosty longer.

Step 5: Garnish and serve

Garnish the cocktail with a couple of sage leaves between two cranberries on a cocktail pick. Lay the pick across the rim of the glass or let it rest in the drink. Serve the cocktail right away while it’s cold.

Editor’s Tip: Before you skewer the sage, gently clap the leaves between your palms to release their aroma. It’s an old bartender trick that makes every sip smell like the holidays.

Mistletoe Martini Variations

- Switch up the spirit: Swap gin for the vodka to add some botanical flair. The juniper and herbal notes play very nicely with the sage garnish.

- Jazz up the juice: There are a zillion different cranberry juice blends out there made with cherry, raspberry and apple juice, so pick whichever one suits your fancy. Know that ones with added flavors may result in a sweeter mistletoe martini. Trader Joe’s Wassail Punch is a fun choice too.

- Get creative with the garnish: Spike cranberries on rosemary twigs, freeze the cranberries and float them on top of the drink, or tie up a little bundle of mint. Your imagination is the limit.

- Serve it up: Skip the fresh ice and strain the cocktail into a chilled coupe or martini glass for a more classic martini presentation. It feels a little more elegant for a holiday dinner party.

How to Store Mistletoe Martinis

A shaken mistletoe martini is best enjoyed right away, since ice keeps melting and diluting the drink the longer it sits. The good news is that this drink can easily be made into a batched cocktail, by mixing the base ahead of time and keeping it in the fridge until the party starts. Just leave out the ice and the garnish until you’re ready to serve.

Can you make a batch of mistletoe martinis ahead of time?

You can make mistletoe martinis ahead of time by mixing a big batch of the base in a pitcher. For eight drinks, stir together 2 cups of cranberry juice, 2 cups of vodka, 1 cup of elderflower liqueur and 1 cup of simple syrup, then chill it for at least a few hours. When guests arrive, you can shake individual portions with ice or you can dilute the base by stirring about 1 cup of cold water into the pitcher before pouring it over fresh ice. Skewer your garnishes a few hours ahead and keep them covered in the fridge so the sage stays fresh.

How long does a batch of mistletoe martini last?

A batched mistletoe martini base lasts up to three days in a covered pitcher or jar in the refrigerator. Give it a good stir before serving, since the ingredients can settle.

Mistletoe Martini Tips

What kind of cranberry juice is best for a mistletoe martini?

The best cranberry juice for a mistletoe martini depends on how sweet you like your cocktails, and you’ll want to adjust the simple syrup to match. Unsweetened, pure cranberry juice is super tart, so use the full ounce of simple syrup if you go this route. A 100% juice blend gets its sweetness from other juices like apple or grape, so start with 1/2 ounce to 3/4 ounce of syrup. Cranberry juice cocktail—the classic bar ingredient—already has added sugar, so start with 1/4 ounce of simple syrup, or skip it entirely. Whichever bottle you grab, taste the cocktail as you go.

- Sugar: You’ll need both granulated and brown sugar. White sugar adds sweetness, while brown sugar brings moisture and chewiness to the cookies.

- Eggs: Eggs help bind the dough. Bringing them to room temperature before making the cookie dough will help them mix more smoothly.

- Vanilla: A splash of vanilla rounds out the sweetness and adds subtle warmth.

- Flour: All-purpose flour gives the cookies structure. Spoon it into the measuring cup and level it off to avoid packing in too much.

- Baking soda: This leavening agent helps the cookies spread and gives them a tender texture.

- Salt: A full teaspoon balances the sweetness of the sugars and marshmallow fluff and brings out the peanut butter flavor. Don’t skip it!

- Marshmallow Fluff: Also known as marshmallow creme, this sweet, spreadable filling gives these cookies their signature gooey centers. Regular marshmallows can work in a pinch, but they won’t give you quite the same creamy filling.

Directions

Step 1: Make the cookie dough

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a large bowl, cream the shortening, peanut butter and sugars until they’re light and fluffy, five to seven minutes. Add the eggs, one at a time, beating well after each addition. Beat in the vanilla.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, baking soda and salt. Gradually add the dry ingredients to the creamed mixture, mixing until they’re combined.

Step 2: Fill and shape the cookies

Scoop the dough by tablespoonfuls and arrange the portions on a parchment-lined baking sheet or work surface. Use your palms or the bottom of a drinking glass to flatten each scoop into a disk.

Pipe or spoon about 1 teaspoon of marshmallow fluff onto the center of half the disks, leaving a little space around the edges. Top each with another dough disk, pinching the edges together to seal in the filling.

Gently roll the filled cookies between your palms to smooth the edges, then flatten them slightly. Arrange the cookies 2 inches apart on parchment-lined baking sheets.

Editor’s Tip: A piping bag or zip-top bag with the corner snipped off makes it easy to add neat, even dollops of marshmallow fluff. If using a spoon, lightly coat it with cooking spray to help the sticky marshmallow release.

Step 3: Bake and cool

Bake until the edges are set and the cookies are lightly browned, 12 to 15 minutes. Let the cookies cool on the baking sheets for a few minutes before transferring them to wire racks to cool completely.

Editor’s Tip: For perfectly shaped cookies, place a large round cookie cutter or glass over each cookie immediately after taking it out of the oven. Gently swirl it around the cookie to nudge the edges into a neat circle while the cookies are still warm and soft.

Recipe Variations

- Add a little sparkle: Roll the filled cookie dough balls in granulated sugar before baking them for a sparkly finish and a little crunch around the edges.

- Switch up the nut butter: Replace the peanut butter with creamy almond butter or cashew butter for a different nutty flavor. Choose a conventional, no-stir variety for the best texture.

- Try a pinch of cinnamon: Mix 1/2 teaspoon of ground cinnamon into the dry ingredients for a subtle warmth that makes these peanut butter cookies taste a little like a snickerdoodle and fluffernutter mashup.

How to Store Fluffernutter Cookies

Once completely cooled, store the fluffernutter cookies in an airtight container at room temperature for up to five days. If stacking them, place parchment paper between the layers to keep the marshmallow from sticking.

Can you freeze fluffernutter cookies?

Yes! For the best results, freeze the unfilled cookie dough balls rather than the assembled cookies. Arrange the dough balls on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze until firm, then transfer to a freezer-safe bag or container for up to three months.

When you’re ready to bake, thaw the dough in the refrigerator, flatten it into disks and add the marshmallow fluff as directed. Seal the cookies, shape them and bake them according to the recipe.

Fluffernutter Cookies Tips

What’s the best type of peanut butter to use for cookies?

Creamy, conventional peanut butter is your best bet for baking these fluffernutter cookies. Brands like Jif or Skippy have a consistent texture that makes the dough easy to mix and shape. Natural peanut butter tends to separate, which can make the dough too oily or crumbly. Save the fancy stuff for your morning toast!

Can you use regular marshmallows instead of creme?

Yes! While marshmallow creme gives these cookies their signature gooey center, you can use mini marshmallows instead. Place four or five mini marshmallows in the center of each dough disk, then top them with another disk and pinch the edges to seal them. The marshmallows will melt as the cookies bake, giving you little gooey pockets in every bite.

Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow

Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.

According to Programa, the extension is designed to reduce duplicate data entry by connecting a 3D model in SketchUp with a project’s Schedule in Programa.

Programa’s Schedules function acts as a streamlined alternative to spreadsheets, detailing each item’s code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

The extension runs inside SketchUp and allows designers to link components in the model to matching products in the Schedule.

As a result, designers can track an item from the first 3D sketch through to its final specification, without entering the same information separately in SketchUp and Programa.

From the model, designers can send a component to a chosen Schedule, or link it to a product that is already listed there.

Programa explained that linking to an existing product creates a connection without adding a duplicate line item, keeping the Schedule “clean” as the design is fleshed out.

Before anything is added, designers can review and edit the product’s information.

The Schedule entry combines the details available from the component with anything entered during that review.

Programa said this gives studios a chance to check the specification before it is used for pricing or procurement.

The extension also provides access to Programa’s Product Library within SketchUp.

Designers can place saved 3D models directly into their designs, and use product images as material swatches to bring selected finishes into the model.

In this way, the products (and finishes) a studio has chosen can be seen in the visuals as well as listed in the Schedule.

The process also works in reverse, starting from the Schedule. A product with a compatible 3D model attached can be placed straight into SketchUp.

If there is no model, designers can choose a stand-in from SketchUp’s 3D Warehouse, or from elsewhere in the current model, to represent the product.

Once a component and a product are connected, supported changes can be reviewed and applied in either direction.

For example, adding another copy of a connected chair in SketchUp generates a quantity change, which the designer can then apply to the Schedule.

The company added that changes are presented for review “before the corresponding update is applied”.

This means the model and the specification can move together as a design develops, while the Schedule is only updated once the designer has chosen to apply a change.

Programa stressed that responsibility remains with the studio.

Designers stay in charge of “selecting the right product, checking its details and deciding when the model or Schedule should change”, the company said.

The aim, it explained, is to carry information between the model and the specification rather than make those decisions on the designer’s behalf.

The extension is aimed at studios that model in SketchUp and manage their specifications in Programa.

The Programa extension works with SketchUp desktop on Mac and Windows.

To learn more, visit Programa’s website or its extension setup guide.

Last night my father called. He wants her legal assistance to clear his criminal record from the ’90s, back when I was a kid growing up in Las Vegas. His only run in with the law: an arrest for being the middleman in a cocaine deal. He didn’t technically buy the coke or sell it to anyone. No, not exactly. What he did was introduce the guy who sold it to a couple of other guys, and one of them was a police informant and, well, arrests were made. A short trial followed, and since all three men were Cuban immigrants, they were convicted of federal drug crimes. Each man had to serve prison time, including my father, of course.

The next morning was my long teaching day, but eventually, I did pick up the FaceTime. When my father asked for an update on my message to Kim, without hesitating, I lied and said I’d messaged her on Instagram to no response.

“She just has so many followers,” I said. “I didn’t expect her to answer.”

He groaned and nodded. My lie was good enough.

Then he asked about my brother and my mom in Florida and “her boring husband, João.” I assured him that everyone was fine, and then I asked him if he knew who Reinaldo Arenas was, since I’d just read his 1992 memoir, Before Night Falls. I told my father that Arenas, too, came here on the Mariel Boatlift in 1980, and that he’d written a famous memoir about growing up in Cuba as a gay man living under the Castro regime. But that, sadly, he’d died of an intentional overdose in 1990, after being diagnosed with AIDS and the physical deterioration that followed.

My father hadn’t heard of him. I didn’t expect him to be familiar with Arenas’s writing, since he doesn’t read very well, but I thought that maybe he knew of him, had possibly heard of him from the other refugees—even though 125,000 people migrated on those boats. My assumption might seem silly, but my father is the most charismatic man I’ve ever known. An enthralling storyteller. He would have made an excellent car salesman, or, in another life with some degrees and without the drug conviction, a wonderful litigator.

“How long was the boat ride from Havana?” I asked.

“Oof, about ten hours,” he said. “That boat was slower than a Russian movie.”

The boat was a shrimp boat and when it took off, people wanted to shout, to burst into celebratory howls, but everyone was told to be quiet until they had exited Cuban waters, about 12 miles away. So he and his brothers—Carlos, Papele (Jorge), Pedro, Domingo, Armando, and Eduardo (who succumbed to alcoholism before I could ever meet him)—watched as dolphins and other flying fish leapt through the air, a sight my father had never seen before. And once they reached mile 12, which took ages in the impossibly sluggish boat, my father couldn’t see his island anymore, and everyone was exhausted by then, so there was no cheering after all. No noise. Most of the other passengers had dozed off, and in that unanticipated moment of stillness, my father was suddenly overcome with a deep melancholy, “a tristeza,” he called it, silently watching his home disappear into nothing. At age twenty-nine, it was the first time my father had ever left his island. In the end, the 90-mile journey to South Florida took ten whole hours.

Once the boat landed, there was no big welcome. The truth is some Americans didn’t want them here, and neither did some of the Cubans who were already here. Unlike the more affluent, lighter-skinned Cubans who’d arrived in the US during the earlier waves of immigration, the Marielitos were browner and blacker and gayer and poorer.

The year of the boatlift, because tensions on the island had come to a boil and citizens were causing too much of a ruckus—you know, because of typical dictatorship things like political repression, no free speech, hunger, etc.—Castro finally opened the port of Mariel and granted everyone permission to leave. “Escoria,” the fleeing refugees were labeled by the regime. Scum. Then President Jimmy Carter reluctantly gave his blessing and, like many others, my father gave both his sisters a long hug goodbye and headed north in search of something else, something new, something, anything, a little more free.

***

It’s almost the end of the semester now and my father won’t stop blowing up my phone. Calling twice, sometimes three times a day. The calls might be due to the season: Christmas is next week. After getting so used to years of his absence—once he’d moved out in my teens to start a new family with the next door neighbor—I now chalk up these recent calls to old age, a form of restitution, I suppose. item.description:

Ridley Scottâs Blade Runner opens in 1982 with a scrolling text about outlawed androids and the âBlade Runner Unitsâ sent to shoot them on sight.

âI think âexplanationsâ are the bug-bears of screenplay writing and I like to stay clear of them,â screenwriter Hampton Fancher told Vulture in 2017. The source novel wonât help either: Rick Deckard is a plain old bounty hunter in Dickâs Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968), and blade runner is, as one literature professorâs study guide puts it, âa term which occurs nowhere in the book.â

The story starts in a doctorâs office.

The Doctorâs Smugglers

Alan E. Nourse practiced medicine in Washington state after getting his medical degree from the University of Pennsylvania in 1955, and he wrote science fiction on the side until 1963, when he retired from medicine to write full-time, according to Josephine Riesmanâs history of the title.

In 1974, he published a novel called The Bladerunner. Itâs set in a future where health care is free to those the government deems fit, but the price of treatment is sterilization. Those who are ineligible have to go to black-market doctors, and the couriers who smuggle instruments to those doctors are the bladerunners: âunderground medical supply smugglers who assist black market doctors in providing health care for the ineligible,â as Cornell University Libraryâs exhibit on the novel and the film puts it.

Kirkus reviewed it that fall and described the hero, Billy Gimp, as Docâs âmedical supplier.â

Enter William S. Burroughs

Burroughs got hold of a copy around the end of 1976, and on December 5, his assistant James Grauerholz wrote to Burroughsâs agent that the author had âliked the book very much, and in fact has begun to consider a film treatment for it,â per Vulture.

Burroughs had the treatment done by March 1977 and called it The Blade Runner, splitting Nourseâs one word into two. Itâs pure Burroughs: written as a long explanation of the movie to someone named âB.J.,â packed with a civil war in greater New York and a black market in sperm, and ending with Billy realizing heâs been living in 1914 the whole time.

The film rights were given up after nobody showed any interest in making it. The treatment was later published as a book by Blue Wind Press in 1979, retitled Blade Runner (a movie) to keep it distinct from Nourseâs novel, which is a funny title for a movie nobody was making.

Fancherâs Bookshelf

At the time, Fancher was working on a script of Dickâs novel under working titles like Android, Mechanismo, and Dangerous Days. A few months in, Scott asked him what Deckard actually was and what he should be called, and Fancher didnât know.

âThat night, I was looking through my books and came across a thin little volume by William Burroughs called Blade Runner,â he told Vulture. âBingo! Everybody liked it, then later, we needed a new title other than the ones weâd been considering and Michael Deeley, the producer, said, âItâs staring us right in the face.ââ

According to Scott, the production then approached Burroughs and bought the title for âa nominal fee,â and the end credits of the film thank Burroughs and Nourse âfor the use of the title Blade Runner.â Nothing else of Nourseâs novel made it into the film: no scalpels, no smugglers, no sterilization laws, just the job title for a cop who hunts replicants.

Burroughsâs book did eventually end up in a movie, albeit a strange one. Tom Huckabee, one of its directors, folded it into the 1983 film Taking Tiger Mountain, starring a young Bill Paxton, and according to the Austin Chronicle, he paid $100 for the rights. So Ridley Scott got the title, and Bill Paxton got everything else.

The latest entry in the Blade Runner franchise, a series called Blade Runner 2099, is now streaming on Prime Video.

Stiller pulls off the emotional moments as well as the absurdist comedy.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, emotional impact

It was 2am when Ivan Tozzo picked up his mobile phone and heard his football club's secretary screaming his name.

A plane carrying the Chapecoense team had crashed into a mountain.

Seventy-one people were dead, including 19 of 22 players from the Brazilian club who were on their way to the biggest game in their history.

It would later emerge the plane had run out of fuel and investigators would find the airline and pilot were to blame as the fuel load was insufficient for the flight on 28 November 2016.

But in the early hours, as Tozzo watched the TV news in the changing room at the club's stadium, his only thought was for the players who would not be coming back to this room.

When he sat alone in the club's boardroom after the funerals as the only director still alive, he cried.

That was the moment when Tozzo â who had changed his mind about travelling with the team because he had a sense of unease about the trip - decided he would lead Chapecoense to rise again.

Chapecoense had been travelling to Colombia to play Atletico Nacional of Medellin in the first leg of the Copa Sudamericana final, South America's second most prestigious club tournament.

It was a first continental final for the Brazilian team.

"The team was very motivated, knowing that we were engraving our names inside the history of the club," goalkeeper Jakson Follmann, one of the three surviving players, tells BBC Sport.

Aged 24 at the time, Follmann had also been looking forward to his imminent wedding, little knowing he would be spending two months in hospital instead.

"Everyone was completely proud of everything they were doing, both for the team and for the community of Chapeco and the region," Follmann says.

Commentator Rafael Henzel, who was one of six survivors of the crash but who died in 2019 following a heart attack, described the Copa Sudamericana as the team's "World Cup" and said in 2017 that "if anyone's ever died happy, it was the people on that plane".

The LaMia 2933 flight from Santa Cruz in Bolivia to the Colombian city of Medellin had a journey distance similar to the plane's flying range, but it did not stop to refuel and crashed into a mountain just 18km from its intended destination.

The pilot, Miguel Quiroga, who was also a co-owner of the airline, died in the crash. In a leaked tape, he can be heard warning of a "total electric failure" and "lack of fuel". However, he did not make a formal distress call.

A Bolivian investigation concluded that the pilot and the airline were directly responsible for the crash, while a Colombian investigation said there was no technical failure and blamed the pilot, the airline and Bolivian regulators.

"I don't call it an accident, I say it was a crime that could have been avoided," says Follman, whose right leg had to be partially amputated to save his life.

"It's the crime of not stopping to refuel, the greed to think that he [the pilot] could get there... with the fuel practically finished."

To date, no-one has been found guilty in relation to the crash.

At the time, Bolivia did not have a system for prosecuting companies. Even when such a facility was introduced in 2021, it did not cover negligent homicide or causing an air disaster.

Charges were brought against individuals in LaMia's management - who denied wrongdoing - but in 2020 a trial was delayed by jurisdictional disputes and difficulties involving defendants who were abroad.

A number of key details about the disaster were established early on.

- At 21:16 local time, the aircraft displayed a low fuel warning but flew on without the crew alerting local authorities.

- Fourteen minutes later, the plane began its descent to Medellin airport but was put in a holding pattern.

- At 21:49, the crew requested priority permission to land, vaguely citing "problems with fuel".

"I remember the lights went out suddenly; then I started praying, asking God to help us," recalled defender Neto, the last of the survivors to be found.

"But a lot of people thought the plane was just landing because it was not an abrupt fall."

Within five minutes, all the engines, drained of fuel, failed.

"Then, I couldn't hear the plane engine any more. It was just a wind. And then an alarm: beep beep beep," Neto told the BBC World Service in 2017.

Seven thousand kilometres away in the small southern Brazilian city of Chapeco, Tozzo watched the scale of the disaster unfold on TV screens at the stadium in the middle of the night.

"At five o'clock in the morning, the players' wives began to arrive. It was despair. People threw themselves on the ground and cried," says Tozzo, a local entrepreneur who was the club's vice-president at the time and had joined the club in 2009 when they were not even playing in Brazil's national football pyramid.

Two days earlier, Tozzo had suffered misgivings about the trip that were so strong that he had changed his mind about travelling to Medellin.

"It was a thing from God. It was not for me to go. I called [financial director] Decio, who organised all our trips, and I told him that I would not go," he says.

"He went crazy with me. 'Why? You agreed to go, now you do not want to go? You have to go.'

"My sister was next to me, saying, 'You need to go to this match, you worked so hard to get to this moment.' But in my head I said, 'No Ivan, I will not go', and I stayed at home."

After the crash, he had another strong feeling about his path.

"I think I had a mission here on Earth to continue Chapecoense after the accident," Tozzo says. "I was the only one of the directors left alive so I took over as [interim] president."

A sleepless week followed in which Tozzo arranged flights to Colombia for doctors, relatives and pastors to identify and recover the remains and be with the survivors.

A memorial service was organised and, in pouring rain, the coffins were brought into Chape's stadium, Arena Conda.…

Chelsea failed at the fundamentals

Bailey: I hope this is not the end for Lyon

AI-GENERATED VOICE: (As Kathy Hochul) We provided luxury accommodations for illegal migrants in beautiful hotels just like this.

JAVAID: The ad, which came with an AI disclaimer, was paid for by Hochul's Republican opponent for the gubernatorial seat, Bruce Blakeman.

(SOUNDBITE OF AD)

AI-GENERATED VOICE: (As Kathy Hochul) This November, don't let Bruce Blakeman lower your taxes or make New York safe. Keep it unsafe and unaffordable with Kathy Hochul as your governor.

JAVAID: Hochul won the race handily by roughly 20 points. More than 90% of the millions of dollars spent on AI ads were supporting Republican candidates, many of whom lost. The ads often did not connect with voters, says Basil Smikle, a Democratic strategist. But he says campaigns will keep using them.

BASIL SMIKLE: You could create an ad that has a lot more shock value than a typical live-action video and produce them more quickly.

JAVAID: They're also much cheaper, says GOP strategist Brian Ruddle.

BRIAN RUDDLE: If you're a candidate who does not have a big budget, can't go out and hire a television production company, but you've got a good message and something that can break through.

JAVAID: That's where AI can help, Ruddle says. And as the technology gets better, it'll get harder to detect what is real.

RUDDLE: It is not just about convincing some people that fake things are real. Sometimes it's about people thinking that real things are now fake.

JAVAID: Jason Riley is a retired Navy pilot from Austin, Texas. He says this time around, the AI ads he saw didn't fool him or sway his vote. But about 61% of Americans are concerned that audio or video deepfakes did affect the election's outcome. That's according to the UC San Diego Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. Some voters are concerned about the technology's ability to misguide them, including Steve Geller (ph), a book editor from Sacramento, California.

STEVE GELLER: I think it's not worth having a society which allows this, even though I do think it can be effective for a politician to use it.

JAVAID: This cycle, AI collected a lot of voter data, which could be useful to campaigns, says Brendan Steinhauser, another GOP strategist.

BRENDAN STEINHAUSER: AI-generated ads that are running to specific individuals based on their behavior online.

JAVAID: That means, he says, very targeted ads at scale that are going to be more effective over time.

Maham Javaid, NPR News.

item.title: Chen Jining: The Tragedy of the ‘Potential Successor’ in Chinese Politics
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Nowadays, political purges in China are nothing new. However, the announcement of an investigation into Shanghai Party Secretary Chen Jining on the night of November 24 still came as a surprise. A model technocrat in charge of China’s economic stronghold, Chen was widely regarded by China watchers as a potential successor to Xi Jinping.

While initially shocking, Chen’s downfall is not overwhelmingly surprising given the continued instability among Chinese political elites. In fact, a survey of the history of comparable regime types suggests that such potential successors are rarely immune to political pitfalls. In some sense, Chen’s case echoes previous instances under communist leaders of similar caliber, like Joseph Stalin and Mao Zedong.

A review of Stalin and Mao’s relations with their potential or designated successors reveals a history of rocky relations. Stalin was infamous for initiating mass purges to weed out “counter-revolutionaries,” “plotters,” and “saboteurs,” labels used to target any perceived sign of disloyalty or ideological deviation. Throughout his rule, Stalin purged anyone who might pose a threat to his authority, regardless of their personal relations with him. Under Stalin, anyone could become an “enemy of the people” overnight; his victims include longtime followers, hatchet men, potential successors, and their associates.

Toward the end of his life, Stalin became increasingly suspicious of those around him. While he never formally designated a successor, his deputy Andrei Zhdanov was considered a likely successor until their relationship grew distant in 1948. The Politburo sent Zhdanov to a sanatorium, where he died from a cardiac arrest soon after. After Zhdanov’s passing, Stalin’s lackeys investigated his underlings in Leningrad and several were executed by shooting, with more imprisoned or sent into exile. The ruthless repression of his confidants indicates that Stalin harbored deep-seated suspicions about Zhdanov’s political network.

Following the Leningrad Affair, Stalin oversaw the Mingrelian Affair that began in 1951, which targeted Lavrentiy Beria, the powerful secret police chief and another possible successor to Stalin. Fortunately for Beria, Stalin died before the Mingrelian Affair reached to its crescendo.

Likewise, Mao treated his successors with equal, if not more, sadism. After the People’s Republic’s establishment in 1949, Mao initially used his deputy and possible successor Gao Gang to attack another potential successor, Liu Shaoqi, before abandoning Gao when his political maneuvers went overboard. Gao committed suicide in 1954 to escape from the subsequent political humiliation rituals.

Although Mao and Liu Shaoqi maintained working relations for the next few years, their relations soured following Liu’s criticism against Mao’s Great Leap Forward in 1962. In the subsequent years, Mao grew increasingly suspicious of Liu’s expanding political influence, which drove Mao to launch the Cultural Revolution with Liu as the main target. Liu died from mental and physical torture in 1969.

Lin Biao, who succeeded Liu as Mao’s designated successor, came into conflict with Mao after the active phase of the Cultural Revolution. While Lin wanted more political security, Mao believed Lin already wielded enough power. Fearing an impending purge, Lin fled China in 1971 but died when his plane crashed in Mongolia.

Although never designated as Mao’s successor, Deng Xiaoping was widely regarded a capable cadre and a frontrunner to succeed him. Nonetheless, Deng was purged twice: first during the opening of the Cultural Revolution and once more in 1976, when he tried to reverse some of its excess. Wang Hongwen, a Cultural Revolution rebel faction leader, was groomed for a year to be Mao’s successor, then sidelined due to his incompetence.

Toward the end of his life, Mao eventually settled on Hua Guofeng as his heir apparent. However, had Mao lived longer, it is very much possible that Hua, too, might have fallen victim to a purge, particularly because his status as Mao’s successor would have attracted a political following among the elite – one that would inevitably have elicited misgivings from the Helmsman.

Although no autocrat can govern alone, the accumulation of authority by capable subordinates can create suspicion and ultimately lead to confrontations. As illustrated in the above examples, potential or designated successors in these political systems enjoy little protection from the ire of the supreme leader. Competence in a successor is not exactly a virtue, but can be a source of distrust, as it poses a challenge to the incumbent leader’s standing.

We may not know the precise reasons behind Chen Jining’s purge for some time, but there is certainly more to the story than the terse official explanation of “severe violations of discipline and law.” Judging from historical precedents, Chen’s status and reputation may have triggered Xi’s suspicion, leading to his removal.

Over the years, prominent politicians, CEOs, and academics who knew Chen have publicly praised him in front of the Chinese media as a young, competent technocrat and a possible future leader of China. Yet outside observers overlooked a crucial point: only Xi can determine who succeeds him, regardless of foreign opinions and declarations. In this system characterized by highly personalized authority, Xi exercises absolute power over the rise and fall of officials. International support for Chen might have hurt rather than helped his image in Xi’s eyes.…
